title: The Tiger, the Brahmin and the Jackal
summary: A kind man finds a trapped beast in a box and must decide how to help.
coverScene: A clever jackal speaks to a tiger trapped inside an old cage while a gentle brahmin watches.

sentences.text: Once upon a time, a big animal was caught inside a strong building.
The building was made of hard material.
He had been kept there for a long time by local people.
These people wanted to protect their home from danger.
The animal wanted to get out very badly.
However, the door was locked close.
Soon, a poor man walked past the building on his way through the forest.
The animal saw him and cried out.
The animal asked the man to let him out of that dark place.
The man felt very sorry for the individual.
He stopped to think about what he should do.
The animal promised that he would never hurt anyone if he were set free.
Trusting his word, the kind man opened the heavy door.
He let the animal step outside into the open air.
However, the bad animal immediately jumped toward the man.
The animal said he wanted to eat him for lunch today.
The worried man asked the animal why he would do such a bad thing.
He asked this after being saved by the kind person.
The animal replied that this was just how the world worked.
He added that everyone would act the same way in this case.
They agreed to ask three different things in the forest.
They wanted to see if that strange rule was true.
First, they asked a big tree.
The tree told them that people were always bad and hurt nature.
Next, they asked a road.
The road gave the same answer about how bad people could be.
Finally, they met a quick dog who wanted to understand the whole story.
The bright dog acted like he could not understand the situation.
He pretended he did not know how a huge animal could fit inside.
The animal wanted to show him how it happened.
So the animal walked right back into the building.
Quickly, the quick dog shut the heavy door.
He locked it close again.

They remembered when the big animal tried to play a game with the man.

They understood that not every living thing in the forest could be trusted.

Therefore, people must always use their head and think before they act in life.
This important lesson has been passed down through generations of families living near the woods.
Even today, parents tell this story to their children before they go to sleep.
It remains one of the most famous stories in the entire region.
Everyone agrees that being nice is good, but being careful is also very important.
The forest remains green and quiet.

sentences.text: Once upon a time, a large animal was caught inside a strong iron room.

The animal wanted to get out very badly, but the door was locked tight.
Soon, a poor man walked past the room on his way through the forest.
The animal saw him and cried out, please let me out of this dark trap.
The man felt very sorry for the creature and stopped to think about what he should do.
The animal promised that he would never hurt anyone if he were set free.
Trusting his word, the kind man opened the heavy door and let the animal step outside.
However, the bad animal immediately jumped toward the man and said he wanted to eat him for lunch.
The frightened man asked the animal why he would do such a bad thing after being saved.
The animal replied that this was just how the world worked and that everyone would act the same way.

sentences.text: Deep within the labyrinthine embrace of the primeval forest, a magnificent yet terrifying creature languished in confinement.
Imprisoned within the cold, unrelenting bars of a heavy iron cage, the great beast had endured countless hours of solitary despair.
The local villagers had constructed this formidable trap to safeguard their fragile homes from his relentless predations.
Now, his amber eyes burned with a singular, desperate longing for the lost liberty of the open canopy.
It was precisely at this fragile juncture that a destitute Brahmin happened to traverse the winding forest path, seeking solace in the quietude of the trees.
Catching sight of the fragile human form, the tiger raised a melodious, pleading voice that belied his savage nature.
He cried out, begging the traveler to release him from the suffocating darkness of his iron tomb.
Struck by profound pity, the pious man halted his steps, torn between instinctive fear and overwhelming compassion.
The beast offered a solemn oath, swearing upon the spirits of the woods that he would never inflict harm upon any living soul if granted his freedom.
Impelled by misplaced trust, the unfortunate Brahmin slid back the cumbersome bolt, allowing the heavy door to swing open.
No sooner had the iron barrier cleared the threshold than the ungrateful predator lunged forward with terrifying velocity.
Snarling fiercely, the tiger announced his intention to consume his savior as a belated morning meal.
Paralyzed by sudden terror, the trembling man demanded to know how the creature could commit such a monstrous act of betrayal after being saved.
The beast merely sneered, asserting that gratitude was an illusion and that ruthless self-interest governed the natural world entirely.
Desperate to delay his imminent doom, the Brahmin proposed that they consult three impartial arbiters of the forest to determine the universal validity of such cruelty.
Their first inquiry was directed toward a towering banyan tree whose ancient branches cast deep, melancholic shadows across the earth.
The venerable tree sighed heavily, declaring that mankind deserved no mercy because humans constantly exploited nature while offering nothing in return.
Disheartened by this verdict, the pair turned toward a dusty pathway that wound its way through the dense undergrowth.
The weary road echoed the exact sentiment, noting that travelers constantly abused its surface before discarding their burdens without a second thought.
Just as hope was entirely extinguished, a clever jackal trotted into view, eager to unravel the strange dispute unfolding before him.
Feigning absolute ignorance, the astute canine tilted his head and professed complete inability to comprehend how such a massive animal could possibly fit inside the cramped iron enclosure.
Irritated by the small creature's perceived stupidity, the proud tiger demanded that he is shown the exact arrangement to prove the reality of his confinement.
Without a moment of hesitation, the great beast strode back into the dim interior of the cage and settled into his original position.
Quick as lightning, the clever jackal slammed the heavy iron door shut and shoved the massive bolt securely into place.
The tiger roared in helpless rage, realizing too late that his arrogance had delivered him back into eternal captivity.
The Brahmin watched the swift reversal of fortune with breathless astonishment, marveling at the sudden restoration of his safety.
Although the process of securing the heavy lock required considerable effort, the jackal labored until the iron mechanism held firm.
The trapped beast hurled his immense weight against the bars, but the reinforced structure refused to yield an inch to his furious assault.
Turning to the bewildered traveler, the jackal remarked that the natural order had finally been restored and that the nearby village was safe once more.
The two companions retraced their steps toward civilization, eager to share the wondrous tale of quick wit triumphing over brute strength.
News of the remarkable event spread rapidly through the settlement, transforming the clever jackal into an undisputed hero.
Grateful villagers ensured that the small canine never lacked for sustenance, showering him with daily gifts of food and affection.
The Brahmin, too, visited his furry savior frequently, forging a deep and lasting bond that endured for the remainder of their days.
Whenever evening descended upon the valley, parents gathered their children close to recount the lesson of the iron room.
They taught the younger generation that while compassion is a noble virtue, it must always be tempered with discernment and caution.
Years drifted by like falling leaves, yet the memory of the strange encounter remained vivid within the collective consciousness of the village.
The old iron room stood silently in the deep forest, serving as a permanent monument to the perils of misplaced trust.
Travelers passing along the nearby road would invariably cast a nervous glance toward the rusted bars and quicken their pace.
The poor man lived out his remaining years in peaceful reflection, deeply grateful for the second chance he had been granted.
He understood profoundly that the world contained dangers which no amount of idealism could ever completely eradicate.
During harsh winter nights, the hearth fire crackled brightly as families huddled together to hear the timeless narrative once again.
Inquiring minds among the youth always asked how the small jackal managed to outsmart such a formidable adversary.
The elders would smile knowingly, reiterating that true wisdom lies in combining swift intelligence with calm observation.
Visitors arrived from distant provinces simply to gaze upon the legendary cage and ponder the strange events of that fateful afternoon.
Each listener departed with a renewed appreciation for the delicate balance between kindness and self-preservation.
Thus, the great tale endured through the ages, whispered from one generation to the next like a precious heirloom.
The deep forest kept its ancient secrets hidden beneath a canopy of emerald leaves, indifferent to the human dramas unfolding beneath its boughs.
Peace settled permanently over the community, undisturbed by any further threats from the shadowed wilderness.
The jackal rested comfortably near the hearth of his human friends, revered by all who knew his remarkable story.
And the world continued its endless rotation, forever offering new lessons to those wise enough to listen.
